newsitem.title: USA: Compaq, Tandem seen as good match-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Compaq, Tandem seen as good match-analysts.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp's unexpected $3 billion deal to buy Tandem Computers Inc is a key step for the personal computer maker as it seeks to expand beyond PCs and a good match for both, analysts said.
Compaq, the world's leader in PCs, has stated since 1995 that it plans to become one of the top three computer makers in the world, with $40 billion in revenues by the year 2000.
"Given their Year 2000 ambitions of being a computer company with a capital C, they clearly had to do something," said Daniel Kunstler, a J.P. Morgan analyst.

"There are no silver bullets, but of the stuff that is available, Tandem is a good one," Kunstler said. "Buying Digital had the possibility of being a disaster and I prefer this to spending $7 billion for Gateway (2000 Inc)."

Compaq and Digital Equipment Corp held merger talks in both 1995 and 1996, with Digital's services business one of Compaq's key areas of interest. And in April, Compaq had reached a nearly $7 billion deal to buy Gateway 2000, the direct marketer of PCs, until its founder Ted Waitt backed out at the last minute. Compaq's CEO Eckhard Pfeiffer declined to comment, calling these deals "all rumors and nothing else."

Analysts see the match as mostly positive, because even though Tandem's emphasis is on the high-end corporate enterprise market with its Himalaya family of fault-tolerant systems, it is also developing powerful servers running Microsoft Corp's Windows NT software.

And Compaq, which is making big inroads in the Windows NT server market, wants to expand into the corporate enterprise market with big systems that can run entire organizations. Tandem's work with NT technology and a technique called clustering will let Compaq build even bigger, more powerful servers, at a lower cost because of Compaq's efficiencies.

"They are clearly going to get technology from Tandem and vice versa because Compaq knows how to make things cheap," said Mark Specker, a SoundView Financial analyst. "There will clearly be some synergies that develop around manufacturing."

"I think it's a good match," said Daniel Ries, a Nomura Research analyst. "It will enable them to make PC servers that no one else can make a little sooner. They can use the great Tandem technology to make servers as competitive as high-end mainframes and UNIX-based servers."
Analysts said Tandem's sales, which are about 75 percent Himalaya-based, will eventually increase to more NT systems.

But the transition in corporate information system departments away from mainframe computers and UNIX-based systems is a slow one, because the NT operating environment is not yet stable or reliable enough for companies with systems that absolutely cannot go down, such as banks, airlines and stock markets.

"We have been selling in the lower level here, starting with file and print servers," Pfeiffer said in an interview. "The point is we (Tandem and Compaq) are growing together here. It will all eventually be the open Intel architecture."
